question.text: Let <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>N</mi></math> be the set of natural numbers and a relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> on <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>N</mi></math> be defined by <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi><mo>=</mo><mfenced close="}" open="{"><mrow><mfenced><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>,</mo><mi>y</mi></mrow></mfenced><mo>∈</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>×</mo><mi>N</mi><mo>:</mo><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>-</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>x</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mi>y</mi><mo>-</mo><mi>x</mi><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>2</mn></msup><mo>+</mo><mn>3</mn><msup><mi>y</mi><mn>3</mn></msup><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow></mfenced></math>. Then the relation <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mi>R</mi></math> is

options.text: symmetric but neither reflexive nor transitive
reflexive but neither symmetric nor transitive
reflexive and symmetric, but not transitive

solution.text:
x3-3x2y-xy2+3y3=0

⇒xx2-y2-3yx2-y2=0

⇒x-3yx-yx+y=0

Now, x=y ∀x,y∈N×N so its a reflexive relation.
But not symmetric & transitive

Since, 3,1 satisfies but 1,3 does not.

Also 3,1&1,-1 satisfies but 3,-1 does not.
